title: Cool Roofs and City Heat
subject: rla
passage:
On summer afternoons, a dark roof can become much hotter than the air above it. The reason is simple: dark surfaces absorb much of the sunlight that reaches them and convert that energy into heat. Some of the heat moves into the building below, while some warms the surrounding air. Across a neighborhood, thousands of sun-heated roofs and paved surfaces can contribute to what researchers call the urban heat island effect, in which developed areas become warmer than nearby places with more vegetation and less pavement.

One response is the “cool roof,” a roof designed to reflect more sunlight and release absorbed heat more efficiently. The idea does not require a roof to feel cold. Instead, the surface stays cooler than a conventional dark roof under the same sunny conditions. A reflective coating, a light-colored membrane, or certain roofing materials can all increase a roof’s ability to reflect solar energy. On a hot day, that difference can reduce the amount of heat passing into the rooms below.

The effect inside a building depends on several factors. Insulation, roof design, local weather, and the amount of direct sunlight all matter. In a well-insulated building, changing the roof may have a smaller effect on indoor temperature because insulation already slows heat transfer. In a poorly insulated building, the difference can be more noticeable. A cooler roof can also reduce how often an air conditioner must run, although the exact savings vary from building to building.

Cool roofs are not a perfect answer for every place. In colder climates, a dark roof can provide a small amount of useful heat during sunny winter days. Snow cover, long cloudy seasons, and local energy prices can also change the calculation. For that reason, building planners usually consider the entire year rather than only the hottest week of summer. They may compare expected cooling savings with any possible increase in winter heating.

Researchers also look beyond a single building. If many roofs in the same area reflect more sunlight, less heat may be stored across the neighborhood during the day. That can help limit local heat buildup, especially when cool roofs are combined with shade trees, parks, and other measures. Still, a roof coating cannot replace those strategies. Trees provide shade and release water vapor, while parks reduce the amount of heat-storing pavement. Each approach works differently.

For homeowners and city planners, the main lesson is not that every roof should be painted white. It is that roof color and material are part of a larger energy and heat-management system. A successful plan considers the building, the climate, and the surrounding neighborhood. Cool roofs are most useful when they are treated as one practical tool among several rather than as a universal fix.

questions.explanation: The passage repeatedly explains that cool roofs can reduce heat, but their effect varies with insulation, climate, and neighborhood conditions.
questions.rule: A central idea should account for the whole passage, including its limits and qualifications.

options.whyWrong: The passage says cool roofs are only one tool and cannot replace other strategies.

options.whyWrong: The passage does not say a cool roof reduces the need for insulation.
